title: In-house designer or a studio
excerpt: Hire an in-house designer when the work never stops and you can support them. Use a studio for a defined launch, or when you need design and build together.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, a long run of work rather than a single launch.
caption: Shelves that imply the work continues. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a company hire an in-house designer?
faqs.answer: Hire when design work repeats every week and you can support the person with a manager, access to the product, and a way for the work to ship. The role should be one job, not brand, product, and social in a single seat. If the backlog is one launch and then a blank, buy the launch first.

faqs.question: When is a studio the better fit than a hire?
faqs.answer: Use a studio for a defined launch, or when you need design and build together and you do not have both inside. A designer without someone to build will produce frames that wait. A studio that only hands over a file recreates that wait.

faqs.question: What does support for a solo designer include?
faqs.answer: It includes someone who can judge the work, a path to engineering, and at least occasional critique from another designer. Software is not that support. If you cannot offer it, a studio or a narrow retainer is the more honest structure.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The choice of an in house designer vs agency is a choice about whether the work ever stops. Hire in-house when design is a continuous job and you can support the person who does it. Use a studio for a defined launch, or when you need design and build in the same hands and you do not have both inside.

A single hire will not give you a department. A studio will not sit in your product meeting every day for three years unless you structure it that way. Pick the shape that matches the calendar you actually have.

## Work that does not stop

Some companies generate design work every week by the nature of the product. New screens, new states, a sales deck that has to match the product, a site that changes when the offer changes. If that week repeats, and you can see the next six months of it, you have a job. Hire for the job.

The job should be describable. Product design for a single interface. Or brand and site for a company that ships campaigns. Or a hybrid, if you are honest about the hours. A role that says "brand, product, web, social, and the pitch deck" is three jobs. One person will do the loudest one and apologize for the rest.

Look at the backlog before you open the role. If the backlog is one launch and then a question mark, you do not yet have continuous work. You have a launch. Buy the launch. Hire when the launch creates a weekly practice you can point at: tickets, pages, or a roadmap of screens.

Ballarat Box Sports and Wabisabi, public Hanabi projects, are the shape of defined site work. They did not require the client to become a design employer first. A product like Got Next or Leadly, where the interface is ongoing, is closer to the in-house case once the company is ready to support it. The studio can start that interface. The weekly continuation is a staffing question, not a moral one.

## What support means

A designer without support is a person asked to invent the company in public, alone. Support is specific.

- A manager who can judge the work and defend the time.
- Access to the product, the customers, and the person who writes the offer.
- Another craft in the company, usually engineering, so the design can ship. If you hire a designer and have no one to build, you have hired a document author.
- Tools and a budget for type, a small photo practice, and the software. Figma is the usual place the work lives. It is not the support.
- A peer, even a part-time one or a studio on a narrow retainer, so critique is not only the founder's taste.

If you cannot offer most of that, the hire will struggle and you will call the struggle a hiring miss. Often it is a support miss. A studio is sometimes the honest substitute: the critique, the build, and the continuity live in the studio, and your company supplies the decisions and the facts.

Pay and seniority should match the "only designer" problem. A first hire who is expected to set the system, design the product, and produce the site is a senior job even when the company is small. Hiring a junior into that seat because the salary is easier will slow the launch and exhaust the person. If the salary you can offer is junior, pair it with a studio that holds the system, and let the hire grow inside a frame.

## A defined launch

A launch has an edge. A new site, a first product surface, a rebrand you can describe, a shop rebuild. When the edge is real, a studio is the right instrument. You get a group that has done the path before, for the length of the path, and then you stop or you continue on purpose.

The studio should design and, when the work is a site or a product interface, build. Hanabi does both. Production work uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, with Motion when the interaction needs it, on Vercel. Design work uses Figma, Framer, and Illustrator. You are not hiring a concept that another unknown team must interpret, unless you already have that team and the handoff is the point.

Define done. The pages, the repo in your accounts, the type and the mark in files you can open, and the portal where brand files, docs, and updates stay after delivery. A launch that ends in a presentation is not a launch. A launch that ends in a site you can edit is.

After a defined launch, wait. See what work actually repeats. Then hire, if the repetition is real and you can support the person. Hiring in the same week you sign the studio, "so we have someone to take it over," often creates a spectator. Let the launch finish. Hire into a system that exists.

## Design and build together

The reason to prefer a studio over a lone in-house designer, early, is the build. An in-house designer who cannot ship will produce frames. The frames will wait on engineering time the company does not have. The site will stay wrong in public while the file looks excellent.

If your engineers are strong and available, an in-house designer can pair with them and you may not need a studio for the interface. That is the best version of the hire: a designer inside, builders inside, a shared backlog. If your engineers are the product and they are already late, adding design work to their queue is a wish. A studio that builds is how the site or the first flow gets out without pretending.

Do not hire a designer to manage a studio as their first act, unless managing vendors is the job you meant. Some founders do want a creative director inside and makers outside. That works when the inside person has authority and time. It fails when they are new, the studio is new, and nobody owns the sentence.

Ask the studio who builds. If the answer is a partner you will never meet, you are coordinating a split. If the answer is the same team that designs, you are buying the shorter loop. Compare that to the in-house alternative with the same question: who will turn this frame into a page next month?

## The lonely seat

The failure mode of the early hire is loneliness. They have no one to review the work who shares the craft. The founder reviews from anxiety. The engineer reviews from feasibility. Both reviews matter. Neither replaces a designer saying the type is doing too much.

You can rent that review without hiring a second full-time person. A monthly critique with a studio, a retainer for the hard screens, or a contract for the brand system while the hire owns the product week. The hire needs a defined ownership or they become a producer of other people's files. Write down what they own.

The failure mode of the studio-only path is memory. The site launches, the engagement ends, and six months later nobody can match the type. The portal and the files exist to prevent that, and someone inside still has to care. Name that someone, even if they are not a designer. A founder who can publish a sentence and knows when to call is enough for a quiet period. A founder who will not look at the site should not skip the hire and also skip the retainer. The site will rot.

[Nielsen Norman Group's page-time research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a useful picture of why rot matters. People often leave in the first 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value has to be visible inside about 10 seconds if you want them to stay. That test is not a launch-day ceremony. Every time the offer changes, the first screen has to pass it again. Someone has to own that pass. A supported in-house designer can. A studio can, on a retainer or a new fixed piece of work. An unsupported hire will get to it after the deck, the social posts, and the founder's last-minute request.

## A sequence that usually works

Start with the launch you can describe. Use a studio if you need design and build and you do not have them. Finish the handoff as part of done.

Run the next two months with the lightest process that keeps the first screen true. If the edits are rare, do them as small fixed pieces. If the edits are weekly and important, start a retainer with the same studio or hire.

Hire when the weekly work is obvious and the support is real: a manager, a way to ship, and a scope that is one job. Keep the studio for the overflows that should not land on a single person: a new brand system, a rebuild, a hard product bet where you want a second senior pair.

Introduce them on purpose. The in-house designer should inherit the files, the repo, and a walkthrough, not a cold folder. The studio should know the hire is the point of contact. Territory should be written down. Product screens belong to the hire. The marketing site belongs to the studio until a date. Or the reverse. Ambiguous territory is how both sides redo the same homepage.

Leaving a studio for a hire is a success, not a slight, when the work has become continuous. Leaving a hire for a studio is also reasonable when the role was a launch in disguise. The expensive version is keeping both at full cost and still not knowing who owns the sentence.

Before either seat spends a quarter on color, the offer has to be stable enough to design. Whether you settle a small identity first or put the site up and let the identity follow is the next decision: [brand first or site first](/blog/brand-first-or-site-first).

Defined launches and longer interface work are both visible in Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
